fatal_errors: The proposed HEA coating is not the target intervention of liquid-metal dealloying a directionally segregated WTaVTi precursor in molten Cu.

The hypothesis incorrectly treats an existing W–Cu composite with service-induced voids as the initial material; the target begins with an as-cast single-BCC WTaVTi alloy whose Ti/V-rich channels are selectively replaced by Cu.
It omits the essential 1200 °C, 96 h vacuum-sealed processing condition and the resulting bicontinuous aligned RHEA–Cu architecture.

The proposed diffusion-barrier/high-entropy mechanism does not reproduce preferential Ti–Cu exchange, retention of W/Ta/V ligaments, or formation of the approximately 300 nm W-rich passivating interlayer.

Neither cited source demonstrates that a CoCrFeNiCu coating suppresses voids or improves thermal conductivity at a W/Cu interface under irradiation; one concerns HEA particles in Al and the other TiC-dispersed W.

The irradiation claim is generalized to fusion-joint service, whereas the target evidence is limited to 25 keV He+ screening of precursor dendrites rather than direct irradiation of the finished composite.
explanation: The response offers a conceptually testable but highly speculative alternative rather than reconstructing the reported materials strategy. Its only substantive agreement is the broad prediction that improved interfacial integrity could raise conductivity relative to an untreated control. It misses the WTaVTi precursor, selective liquid-metal dealloying, directional Cu-channel formation, W-rich interlayer, quantitative thermal behavior, and restricted irradiation evidence. The proposed paired control experiment could test the coating hypothesis, but lacks specified temperatures, fluences, coating dimensions, orientation controls, and quantitative acceptance thresholds. Most importantly, the supplied literature does not validate the proposed HEA-coated W–Cu intervention or its mechanism.
